title: Sloth and diligence
hook: the monks' noonday demon: listless boredom with good things

segments.voice: Yesterday, wrath and patience: Jonah's fury, and God's question. Your line was slow to anger. Did you count to ten? Day one thousand two hundred four.

It's the middle of the day in the Egyptian desert. A monk sits in his small cell. He came out here on purpose, to pray, to work, to be with God. And right now he can't stand it. He looks out the door at the sun, and the sun hasn't moved. He looks again. Still hasn't moved. The day feels endless. He starts thinking another monastery would suit him better, or a visit to a brother would do him good, or maybe this whole life was a mistake. Nothing is wrong. That's the trouble. The old monks had a name for this hour, and a name for this feeling. Today's word: acedia.

Tradition says acedia is the old name behind the sin later called sloth. And it's a different animal from laziness. A lazy person might be happily asleep on the couch. Acedia is not happy. It's a heavy, restless boredom with the very things that matter: prayer, work, the people in front of you. Evagrius, a monk who lived in that desert and wrote about the thoughts that trouble monks, called it the noonday demon. He described it the way the hook did: the monk staring at the sun, the day stretching out, the itch to be anywhere else. Some of the monks connected it with a line in the Psalms about a destruction that wastes at noonday. Noon is the right hour for it. The morning's fresh start is gone. The evening's rest is far off. It's the long middle, where a lot of life is actually lived. And the cure the monks gave was not a burst of effort. It was staying put. Stay in your cell, they said. Don't run. And do the next small thing with your hands. Weave a basket. Say a psalm. Sweep. Scripture has its own blunt version: "Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise." The ant doesn't wait to feel inspired. And Ecclesiastes says, "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might." Whatever your hand finds. Not the great task. The one in front of you. That's diligence: not hustle, but care that keeps showing up. And looking back over this week, the same shape keeps appearing. Justice, courage, temperance, humility, kindness, patience, and now diligence: each one a small, steady habit, practiced one ordinary day at a time.

Here's the practice: do the next small task. Settle, and breathe. Notice if there's a flat, heavy feeling anywhere in your day, a thing you keep circling and not starting. Don't fight it, and don't make a plan to fix your whole life. Just find the next small task. One email. One dish. One page. Name it to yourself. If you pray, you can offer the task, as the monks did with their baskets. When the bell rings, get up and do that one thing. The bell holds the time.
Acedia. The desert monks' word for listless boredom with good things, the noonday demon; the old root of sloth.
Your line: the noonday demon. Today, when the afternoon goes flat and you want to be anywhere else, stay, and do the next small thing your hand finds. Day one thousand two hundred four.

howItsDone: In Christian monastic tradition, acedia is met with stability and steady work: staying in one's place, keeping the hours of prayer, and doing ordinary tasks with care; the deadly sin of sloth in later lists grew from it.

notes: Evagrius on acedia (Praktikos 12) is paraphrased: the monk watching the sun, the day seeming long, the urge to leave for another place. His specific numbers (e.g. the day seeming fifty hours long) are left out under the claims rule. Confirm.

Psalm 91:6: the KJV reads 'the destruction that wasteth at noonday'; the Greek Septuagint (Psalm 90:6) reads a 'noonday demon'. The script says only that 'some of the monks connected it with a line in the Psalms'. Confirm phrasing.
'The cure the monks gave': stay in the cell and do manual work; attributed generally to desert tradition (Evagrius; Cassian, Institutes 10, on manual labor). Confirm.
'Acedia is the old name behind the sin we now call sloth' is a historical claim (the eight thoughts became the seven deadly sins, with acedia folded into sloth); confirm.
Week end (days 1198–1204) looks back at justice, courage, temperance, humility, kindness, patience and diligence.
Original: ἀκηδία; the gloss 'a not-caring' rests on the lexicon (a- + κῆδος); confirm.
